title: Chris Vazquez
text:
Hi, I’m Chris! I’m based in Boston, and I love using data to answer questions and turn them into stories people can follow.
I hold an M.S. in Political Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where my research focused on representation, local politics, and institutions. Before MIT, I earned a B.A. in Political Science from Brigham Young University.
I’m currently looking for roles in data science and data analytics. You can see some of what I’ve been working on in my projects.
Outside of work, I really enjoy watching movies and sports! Go Cougs and go Heels!

title: Projects
text:
Race in Local Government Meetings
    
    
    I used a large language model to classify transcripts from more than 8,000 city council meetings, measuring how race comes up in local deliberation and whether a council’s racial composition changes it.
    
    
    Abstract | Full Paper | Read more
    
    
    
      Does a city council’s racial composition affect what is discussed in council meetings? Studies of local politics infer these effects from policy outcomes, but a council settles what counts as a problem in public meetings before it decides anything. To measure what councils discuss, I classify transcripts from over 8,000 meetings with a large language model, recording whether race is engaged, whether symbolically or substantively, and which of six policy areas it concerns. Race is a small and concentrated share of local deliberation, arises more often in deciding something than in honoring a group, and shifts with council composition in volume and in focus. Regression discontinuity and two-way fixed effects designs each rule out effects larger than nearly all the year-to-year movement cities record. This paper supplies an empirical foundation for future work, a measure of what councils attend to and the scale any effect must reach to be found.
    
    
  

  
    
    
    
    The Party Never Ends?
    
    Evidence of Nationalization in Local Politics
    
    
    Using an original survey and principal component analysis, I find that people’s local policy preferences divide along partisan lines, a sign that national partisanship reaches into local politics.
    
    
    Abstract | Full Paper
    
    
    
      Is American local political behavior becoming nationalized? Nationalization suggests that local political behavior also has partisan elements. However, local government and politics have a lot of nonpartisan elements, and previous research in local political behavior relies on measures of national policy preferences from mass surveys. It is still unknown if there is a relationship between national and local preferences. One potential relationship is that individuals could evaluate local policies in a partisan lens when they only operate in a national context. To test the role of context in local policy preferences, I conducted an original survey that primes respondents with different contexts to influence local policy preferences. Despite the experiment being ineffective, I find through principal component analysis that there are divisions in local policy preferences that align with respondents’ partisanship. This finding illustrates that partisanship could also define local policy preferences as it does national preferences.
    
    
  

  
    
    Oh No! I’ve Accidentally Elected a Republican!
    
    The Effects of Nonpartisan Local Elections on City Council Partisan Composition
    
    
    Using data on cities’ electoral institutions and the partisanship of officials and residents, we find that nonpartisan elections let candidates from a city’s less popular party win council seats.
    
    
    Abstract | Poster
    
    
    
      Does the use of nonpartisan elections in local elections impact partisan representation on city councils? In nonpartisan elections, voters cannot rely on a candidate’s party as a heuristic, so candidates that would affiliate with an unpopular party can run and win elections. Using a dataset of municipal government electoral institutions and a dataset with officials’ and residents’ partisanship, we find that minority party candidates can “sneak” their way into office in cities where their party or ideology is unpopular. Electoral institutions matter when it comes to partisan representation on U.S. city councils.
